messages.body_plain:
Hi

the problem is due to different formulation of a spline in gam and inla.
inla uses all values of 'covariate' and create a discretized version of
an integrated wiener process, for which to many unique values makes it
slow(er) and to close values makes it numerical singular. yours satisfy
both:

> min(diff(unique(sort(Data$covariate))))
[1] 1.929295612e-10

> length(unique(Data$covariate))
[1] 56302

there is a function is 'fix' this, so using

response ~ f(inla.group(covariate), model="rw2")

will solve it; see ?inla.group for details.

Best
H

messages.body_plain:
Dear Help,

Following the Section 4.2 in the R-INLA tutorial: SPDE models, I want to mdoel a suface that has non-linear relationship with the x-coordinate using the effect f(x,model='rw1') and f(i,model=spde). But I have some questions on the 'rw1' part.
1. At the top of Page 41 of the R-INLA tutorial: SPDE models, it is said that
log(\mu_i) = \alpha + \sum_{j=1}^k w_k I(F_i=F0_k) + x_i
which is quite confusing.. For example, what is the subscript 'j'? What are the knots F0_k? Should 'I(.)' function be the indicator function, then for some F_i which is not at the knots (number of knots is less than the covariates F_i?), the effect of this part is zero?
2. In the model without 'rw1', for example, y~intercept + f(i,model=spde), I can have the posterior mean of the response variables in two ways: (1) from the result of the INLA call: res$summary.fitted.values[ind_prd,1] (2) draw a lot of posterior samples from the result using inla.posterior.sample, and calculate the sample mean of the 'sample[[i]]$latent[ind_prd]'. The difference between the two posterior means are relatively small. However, when I add a 'rw1' part in the model, the sample posterior mean in way (2) cannot approximate that in way (1) well. Is that because the way I select the response predictions in the posterior samples is not right? I put a R script for a simple example to illustrate this question.
3. Now I put the estimate and prediction steps together in the inla call. But as suggested in the tutorial, when the dimension is high this can be less efficient. Can I draw correct posterior samples using the result of the model
y~Intercept + f(x,model='rw1') + f(i,model=spde)
with only estimate saying
stk_est <- inla.stack(data=list(resp=z),A=list(A_est,1),effects=...)
f.est <- resp ~ 0 + Intercept + f(x,model='rw1') + f(i,model=spde)
res <- inla(f.est,data=inla.stack.data(stk.est),control..,)
by for example sum of predictor components in the posterior samples?

Thanks a lot!

Best regards,
Xiaoyu

The first block on sample[[.]]$latent corresponds to res$summary.fitted.values. Them all components on res$summary.random[[...]] are added to it.

You rely on this approach as you rely on the interpolation and on sampling.

As the covariate is just one of the coordinates you can have it everywhere. The longitude coordinate on the mesh points is just mesh$loc[,1]

To sample the linear predictor on other locations 'xy1', you also need your covariate on this location. Remember that when you include a prediction stack for a set of locations, inla already returns marginal posterior for each of that locations. So, if you only want simple summaries, having it from these posterior marginal distribution is better than than from sampling (no sampling error).

messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I believe I understand the method by which once can formulate latent state space models. I am not sure, however, of what the weighting factor in the "iid" model is doing when it is set to a negative value. The "iid" documentation does not indicate what negative valued weights do.

For example in FAQ #15 (http://www.r-inla.org/faq#TOC-I-have-a-complicated-state-space-model-can-this-be-fitted-using-INLA- ) the weight is assigned a value of -2:

messages.body_plain:
Hello,

This is a question on implementing an INLA solution to a state space problem. Your patience would be appreciated as I am not a statistician.

In many fields, a discrete form of the Verhulst equation is used to model population dynamics.

A state-space formulation usually involves an observation equation such as:

(1)  O{t} = q * B{t}
(2)  B{t+1} = B{t} + r B{t} ( 1 - B{t} / K ) - H{t}

where:

{t} is time ( in years )
O{t} is the observed index of abundance at time {t}, usually with lognormally distributed errors
B{t} is the unobserved biomass we are trying to estimate, usually assumed to follow a lognormal error distribution
H{t} is the harvest, usually assumed to be known without error
r is the "intrinsic" rate of increase, usually assumed to be Gaussian
K is the asymptotic carrying capacity, usually assumed to be Gaussian or Lognormal
q is a proportionality factor,

Implementation in BUGS is simple. Is it possible to address such problems with the augmented model approach in INLA? If so, would you please point me in the right direction?

Thank you,
Jae

<cut correct looking code>

I'll assume that you have the line
  ind_prd <- inla.stack.index(stk_full, tag="prd")$data
as well.

> Then I can get posterior mean of the response by
> exp(res$summary.fitted.values$mean[ind_prd]), can I?

Not quite, but close.  Note that exp(E(x|y)) is not equal to E(exp(x)|y), so
be careful with transforming expectations.  It's much safer to use the posterior
quantiles instead, as they do transform cleanly, so for a pure point
estimate you can do

  exp(res$summary.fitted.values[ind_prd,"0.5quant"])

to get the posterior median of the response.

> And how can I get the
> correct posterior standard deviation of the response?

You can use inla.emarginal() and related functions for computing
transformed properties of the posterior, operating on
"res$marginals.fitted.values".

Finn

Can anyone point me to an example of how to implement a multinomial logistic regression in a way that allows estimation of coefficients for covariates (and thus prediction into unsampled data points)?

Many thanks,

Tom Bird

And also in the original inla paper

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

How to do it depends on the _kind_ of seasonal model you need.
If the seasonal effects are allowed to be independent, you might be able to
use something like

f(location, model="bym") + f(hourindex, model="somecyclicalmodel", replicate=dayindex)

with some additional constraints to make it identifiable.
If the seasonal effects need to be coupled with the bym model, something like

f(location, model="bym", group=hourindex,
  control.group=list(model="somecyclicalmodel"))

would be needed instead.
In both cases, "somecyclicalmodel" would be whatever your seasonal model should be (but only some models are supported by the "group" feature), e.g. "generic0", with precision matrix for a cyclic RW1 or RW2 model, or perhaps as simple as "iid"; as this is a problem-specific modelling choice, it's hard to give very specific advice for that. (I'm not sure what the "seasonal" latent model should be interpreted as, but suspect that it is not the type of model you want.)

All of the above assumed that the only temporal part of the model would be the seasonal effects.  It may become more complicated if you need a full spatio-temporal model with interactions between all space and time components.

Finn L

Have you checked the parameter estimates, and used verbose=TRUE to
check the parameter optimisation?  The time per likelihood evaluation
should be monotone in the mesh size, but the number of iterations
needed doesn't necessarily behave in a predictable way.

The precise structure of the model also has an effect, and it sounds
like you changed more than only the mesh size (e.g. the locations of
the data points affects the parameter estimation, and hence the
optimiser).

Finally, inla uses different computing strategies for different model
sizes, and it may be that it doesn't always use the optimal strategy.

messages.body_plain:
Dear INLA,

first of all thank you so much for developing the code for this suite of models. I'm fairly new to the INLA approach, but the models are really interesting, so apologies for the naive questions.

I have binomially distributed data, and I would like to estimate the model parameters and project onto a grid. I've been following some examples, and patching together where necessary. This example is inspired by  http://www.math.ntnu.no/~daniesi/Roros.pdf

I first create some random data, with a bit of variability. That's fine and the model is fitted. However I'm unsure how to project the results onto a grid. I pasted some code from the Parana rainfall example, but I've set up "inla.mesh.project" incorrectly, but I'm unsure of the solution.

Any assistance would be greatly appreciated, or an alternative...the grid plot is to view the mean of the random field. In the example the following code is used plot(old.mesh.class(mesh),r$summary.random$data_points$mean)
however old.mesh.class(mesh) is an old function I think. I suspect this plots the mean value. Any thoughts on alternatives?

In my real example I had set up the data as an INLA stack. However with use of the Ntrials in the binomial likelihood, I'm unsure how to set up the data. Could anyone direct me to an example where the data stack is used for a binomial model, and where estimates are projected?

Many thanks,

Kath

library(INLA)
library(boot) #for inverse logit
# Make some fake data
N=100
points = matrix(runif(2*N),ncol=2)
#The ’true’ surface
fcn = function(loc){
  return( cos(loc[,1])*sin(4*loc[,2]))
}
noisy_data = rbinom(N,rep(1,N),inv.logit(fcn(points)))
plot(points,cex=noisy_data+0.5)
## Build a mesh
bnd = inla.mesh.segment(matrix(c(0,0,1,0,1,1,0,1),
                               ncol=2,byrow=TRUE))
mesh = inla.mesh.create(points,boundary=bnd,
                        refine=list(max.edge=0.1))
plot(mesh)
##Make the SPDE
# imatern =
spde = inla.spde.create(mesh,model="imatern")

## Fit the model
fake_data = list(y=noisy_data, data_points = mesh$idx$loc)
formula = y ~ f(data_points, model=spde)-1
r = inla(formula, family="binomial",Ntrials=rep(1,N),
         data=fake_data,verbose=TRUE)
summary(r)
plot(r,plot.random.effects=F)
# out of date function...
#plot(old.mesh.class(mesh),r$summary.random$data_points$mean)

# project a fit to a grid
(stepsize <- 0.1)
(nxy <- round(c(diff(c(0,1)),diff(c(0,1)))/stepsize))
projgrid <- inla.mesh.projector(mesh, xlim=c(0,1),ylim=c(0,1), dims=nxy)
# make the predictions
xmean <- inla.mesh.project(projgrid, r$summary.random$i$mean)
xsd <- inla.mesh.project(projgrid, r$summary.random$i$sd)
